History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
63-year-old male with acute, persistent central chest pressure radiating to left arm/shoulder, associated diaphoresis, dyspnea, and nausea; high suspicion for acute coronary syndrome—ambulance arranged for emergent evaluation.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Central chest “pressure, like someone sitting on my chest,” began while gardening ≈2 hours prior to call; remains ongoing.  
• Radiation: Left arm and left shoulder.  
• Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath, profuse sweating, mild nausea (no vomiting), subjective palpitations.  
• First episode; no previous similar pain.  
• Triggers/relievers: Began during light activity (kneeling in garden); no clear relieving factors reported.  
• Functional baseline: Generally sedentary; does little regular exercise.  
• Review of systems (pertinent):
  – Cardiovascular: Chest pressure as above; palpitations noted.  
  – Respiratory: Dyspnea present.  
  – GI: Nausea without emesis.  
  – No other ROS data provided.

Past Medical History:
• Hypertension (duration not specified; current control status undocumented).

Medications:
• None documented.

Allergies:
• Aspirin – causes swelling (mild allergic reaction). No other drug allergies reported.

Social History:
• Tobacco: Smokes ~10 cigarettes/day for 15 years.  
• Alcohol: ~7–8 pints beer/week.  
• Illicit drugs: Not mentioned.  
• Occupation: Restaurant owner (sushi shop).  
• Living situation: Lives alone.  
• Exercise: Minimal; largely inactive.  
• Weight: Patient acknowledges being overweight.

Family History:
• Father: Fatal myocardial infarction at ~60 years.  
• Mother: “Heart problems” (details not provided).  
• No other family history discussed.

Physical Examination:
Not performed (telehealth call); no vitals available.

Investigations:
• None yet. Plan for pre-hospital 12-lead ECG by ambulance crew. Destination hospital and further studies (cardiac enzymes, imaging) to be determined upon arrival.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Suspected acute coronary syndrome / possible myocardial infarction  
  – High-risk features: Persistent chest pressure, radiation to left arm, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, multiple cardiovascular risk factors (male >60 y, smoker, hypertension, family history, overweight).  
  – Plan:  
    • Emergency medical services activated; ambulance en route.  
    • Pre-hospital ECG and cardiac monitoring.  
    • Convey to emergency department/cardiac center per EMS protocol.  
    • Advise patient to keep front door open for EMS access; remain on line with clinician until arrival.  
    • Communicate aspirin allergy details to EMS/hospital; consider benefits vs. risk of ASA loading despite mild allergy per cardiology guidance.  
    • Anticipate hospital management: serial ECGs, cardiac biomarkers, possible antiplatelet/anticoagulation, nitroglycerin, beta-blocker, statin, reperfusion therapy if STEMI confirmed.

Issue 2: Cardiovascular risk factor modification (long-term)  
  – Hypertension, smoking, overweight, alcohol intake, unknown lipid status.  
  – Plan (deferred until post-acute event):  
    • Formal lipid profile.  
    • Smoking cessation program.  
    • Weight management, diet, exercise counseling.  
    • Alcohol moderation.  
    • Optimize antihypertensive regimen.

Issue 3: Aspirin allergy evaluation  
  – Mild swelling reaction; may tolerate desensitization or alternative antiplatelet therapy.  
  – Plan: Allergy documentation; consider allergist review and risk-benefit discussion post-ACS event.

General plan items:  
• Ensure medication reconciliation on hospital admission.  
• Update emergency contact information given patient lives alone.

Quality checks (document_quality):

Missing/expected elements:
• Current medication list and dosages not obtained.  
• Past surgical history, immunizations, and other medical problems not discussed.  
• No baseline vitals available.  
• No objective physical exam findings.

Internal conflicts:
• Patient age: stated DOB 08/08/1958 (makes him 65 y) yet patient/doctor both mention “around sixty.” (conflict noted).

Transcript quality:
• Clear overall; minor conversational noise but clinically adequate.
